lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Why Mars Sometimes Runs Backward
top_level_objectives: Describe the observational phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion for outer planets
Explain why the geocentric model required epicycles to account for retrograde loops
Explain how heliocentric relative motion between Earth and an outer planet naturally produces the retrograde loop
Relate orbital distance and speed to the size and duration of a planet's retrograde loop
Compare retrograde behavior across Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn

scenes.scene_name: Night Sky Time-Lapse: Mars Against the Stars
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the raw observational puzzle by letting students watch Mars drift and loop against fixed background stars over a simulated multi-week period, exactly as ancient and modern sky-watchers would see it.
key_visuals: A star-filled dome/skybox with constellation outlines labeled
A glowing red marker for Mars leaving a faint trailing path as time advances
An on-screen date/night counter advancing night by night
The path visibly slowing, reversing westward, then resuming eastward motion
student_actions: Scrub or step through a time slider night by night
Mark or trace Mars's position on successive nights
Identify the point where Mars appears to reverse direction
Record observations of how long the reversal lasts

scenes.scene_name: The Geocentric Puzzle: Epicycles on Wheels
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how ancient astronomers modeled retrograde motion within an Earth-centered universe, highlighting the awkwardness of the epicycle solution.
key_visuals: Earth fixed at the center with Mars riding a small circle (epicycle) whose center travels a larger circle (deferent) around Earth
A trace line showing the resulting looped path matching the observed sky motion
Side-by-side comparison of the epicycle-generated loop with the Scene 1 sky trace
student_actions: Rotate the epicycle mechanism forward in time and watch the loop form
Compare the generated loop shape to the recorded sky observations from Scene 1
Answer a prompt on why this model needs an extra circle just to explain one planet's motion

scenes.scene_name: Stepping Outside: The Heliocentric Solar System
scenes.brief_purpose: Shift the viewpoint from Earth's surface to a vantage point above the solar system so students can see both Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun on separate, simultaneous paths.
key_visuals: A top-down or angled view of the Sun with Earth's and Mars's orbital paths drawn as circles/ellipses
Earth and Mars as moving markers with velocity arrows showing relative speeds
A faint sight-line from Earth to Mars projected outward to a distant star background
student_actions: Advance time and watch Earth and Mars move along their orbits
Compare the two orbital speeds visually via the velocity arrows
Toggle between the outside view and the Earth-sky view to link both perspectives

scenes.scene_name: The Overtaking Maneuver: Building the Loop from Relative Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Let students see, in real time, how the projected sight-line from Earth to Mars sweeps backward against the stars precisely when Earth overtakes Mars on the inside track, generating the retrograde loop naturally.
key_visuals: The same top-down orbital view with the Earth-to-Mars sight-line extended to a background star field
A synchronized secondary panel showing the sight-line's intersection point tracing the same loop seen in Scene 1
Highlighted arc segment marking where Earth is directly 'passing' Mars on the inside lane
student_actions: Step time forward slowly through the passing event
Watch the projected sight-line trace the loop on the star field panel
Pause at the moment of closest approach and note it corresponds to the middle of the retrograde loop

scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce the heliocentric explanation with a familiar, intuitive analogy of overtaking a slower car on a highway, making the abstract orbital geometry concrete.
key_visuals: Two simplified cars on parallel curved lanes, one faster (inner) and one slower (outer)
A background of distant roadside poles standing in for background stars
A viewpoint from inside the faster car showing the slower car appear to drift backward against the poles as it's passed
student_actions: Drive/advance the faster car forward through the passing maneuver
Observe the slower car's apparent backward drift against the poles
Map each part of the car analogy (inner/outer lane, passing point) back to Earth and Mars from Scene 4

scenes.scene_name: Comparing Outer Planets: Mars vs Jupiter vs Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the heliocentric relative-motion explanation to Jupiter and Saturn, letting students see how greater orbital distance shrinks the apparent loop.
key_visuals: A shared outside solar-system view showing Earth's orbit plus the orbits of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn at correct relative scale
Three side-by-side sky-trace panels showing each planet's retrograde loop shape and size
A data readout comparing loop duration and angular size for each planet
student_actions: Select each planet in turn to display its orbit and resulting sky loop
Compare loop sizes and durations across the three planets
Answer a guided question relating orbital distance to loop size using the observed pattern

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the lab's arc by having students recap both models side by side and articulate why the heliocentric model is the simpler, more natural explanation for retrograde motion.
key_visuals: Split-screen recap: geocentric epicycle loop on one side, heliocentric overtaking view on the other, both producing the same sky trace
A summary timeline of the full Mars retrograde event annotated with key stages (approach, loop, resume)
A final comparative chart of Mars, Jupiter, Saturn loop characteristics
student_actions: Toggle between the two historical models one final time
Complete a short reflection prompt explaining in their own words why the loop appears without epicycles
Submit answers comparing loop size across the three outer planets to wrap up the lab
